groups.title: Flanders Conference Hotel
groups.instruction: Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

transcript.text: Hello, Flanders conference hotel.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: Oh, hi.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I wanted to ask about conference facilities at the hotel.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Have I come through to the right person?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: You have.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: I’m the customer services manager.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: My name’s Angela.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: So how can I help you?
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: Well, I’m calling from Barrett and Stansons, we’re a medical company based in Perth.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Oh yes.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: And we’re organising a conference for our clients to be held in Sydney.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: It’ll be held over two days and we’re expecting about fifty or sixty people.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: When were you thinking of having it?
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: Some time early next year, like the end of January?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: It’d have to be a weekend.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Let me see … our conference facilities are already booked for the weekend beginning January 28th.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: We could do the first weekend in February?
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: How about January 21st?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I’m afraid that’s booked too.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: Well, let’s go for the February date then.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: So that’s the weekend beginning the 4th.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Now can you tell me a bit about what conference facilities you have?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Sure.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: So for talks and presentations we have the Tesla room.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: Sorry?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Tesla – that’s spelled T-E-S-L-A. It holds up to a hundred people, and it’s fully equipped with a projector and so on.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: How about a microphone?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Yes, that’ll be all set up ready for you, and there’ll be one that members of the audience can use too, for questions, if necessary.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: Fine.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: And we’ll also need some sort of open area where people can sit and have a cup of coffee, and we’d like to have an exhibition of our products and services there as well, so that’ll need to be quite a big space.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: That’s fine, there’s a central atrium with all those facilities, and you can come before the conference starts if you want to set everything up.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: Great.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: And I presume there’s wifi?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Oh yes, that’s free and available throughout the hotel.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Would you also like us to provide a buffet lunch?
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: We can do a two-course meal with a number of different options.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: What sort of price are we looking at for that?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Well, I can send you a copy of the standard menu.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: That’s $45 per person.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: Or you can have the special for $25 more.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: I think the standard should be OK, but yes, send me the menu.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Now we’re also going to need accommodation on the Saturday night for some of the participants … I’m not sure how many, but probably about 25.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: So what do you charge for a room?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Well, for conference attendees we have a 25% reduction, so we can offer you rooms at $135.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: Normally a standard room’s $180.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: And does that include breakfast?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Sure.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: And of course, guests can also make use of all the other facilities at the hotel.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: So we’ve got a spa where you can get massages and facials and so on, and there’s a pool up on the roof for the use of guests.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: Great.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Now what about transport links?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: The hotel’s downtown, isn’t it?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Yes, it’s about 12 kilometres from the airport, but there’s a complimentary shuttle bus for guests.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: And it’s only about ten minutes’ walk from the central railway station.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Now, I don’t know Sydney very well, can you just give me an idea of the location of the hotel?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Well, it’s downtown on Wilby Street, that’s quite a small street, and it’s not very far from the sea.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: And of course if the conference attendees want to go out on the Saturday evening there’s a huge choice of places to eat.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: Then if they want to make a night of it, they can go on to one of the clubs in the area – there are a great many to choose from.
transcript.speaker: ANGELA

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: So if we go ahead with this, can you give me some information about how much …
transcript.speaker: MAN

groups.title: Volunteers and people helped

options.text: rediscover skills not used for a long time

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter for each answer.

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: My name’s Lucy Crittenden, and I’m the Director of Operations for an organisation that arranges volunteering in this part of the country.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I’m hoping I can persuade one or two of you to become volunteers yourselves.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Let me start by briefly explaining what we mean by volunteering.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Volunteers are teenagers and adults who choose to spend some time, unpaid, helping other people in some way.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Most volunteers devote two or three hours to this every week, while a few do much more.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The people they help may have physical or behavioural difficulties, for example.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Volunteers can do all sorts of things, depending on their own abilities and interests.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: If they’re supporting a family that’s struggling, for example, they may be able to give them tips on cooking, or recommend how to plan their budget or how to shop sensibly on their income.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: They might even do some painting or wallpapering, perhaps alongside any members of the family who are able to do it. Or even do some babysitting so that parents can go out for a while.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The benefit from volunteering isn’t only for the people being helped.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Volunteers also gain from it: they’re using their skills to cope with somebody’s mental or physical ill health, and volunteering may be a valuable element of their CV when they’re applying for jobs: employers usually look favourably on someone who’s given up time to help others. Significantly, most volunteers feel that what they’re doing gives them a purpose in their lives.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And in my opinion, they’re lucky in that respect, as many people don’t have that feeling.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Now I’d like to tell you what some of our volunteers have said about what they do, to give you an idea of the range of ways in which they can help people.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Habib supports an elderly lady who’s beginning to show signs of dementia.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Once a week they, along with other elderly people, go to the local community centre, where a group of people come in and sing.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The songs take the listeners back to their youth, and for a little while they can forget the difficulties that they face now.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Our volunteer Consuela is an amazing woman.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: She has difficulty walking herself, but she doesn’t let that stop her.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: She helps a couple of people with similar difficulties, who had almost stopped walking altogether.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: By using herself as an example, Consuela encourages them to walk more and more.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Minh visits a young man who lives alone and can’t leave his home on his own, so he hardly ever saw anyone.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But together they go out to the cinema, or to see friends the young man hadn’t been able to visit for a long time.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Tanya visits an elderly woman once a week.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: When the woman found out that Tanya is a professional dressmaker, she got interested.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Tanya showed her some soft toys she’d made, and the woman decided to try it herself.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And now she really enjoys it, and spends hours making toys.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: They’re not perhaps up to Tanya’s standard yet, but she gains a lot of pleasure from doing it.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Alexei is a volunteer with a family that faces a number of difficulties.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: By calmly talking over possible solutions with family members, he’s helping them to realise that they aren’t helpless, and that they can do something themselves to improve their situation.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This has been great for their self-esteem.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And the last volunteer I’ll mention, though there are plenty more, is Juba.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: She volunteers with a teenage girl with learning difficulties, who wasn’t very good at talking to other people.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Juba’s worked very patiently with her, and now the girl is far better at expressing herself, and at understanding other people.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: OK, I hope that’s given you an idea of what volunteering is all about.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Now I’d like …
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

groups.title: Problems with band members

options.text: makes a lot of mistakes in rehearsals

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter for each answer.

transcript.text: So how are you getting on with your teaching practice at the High School, Joe?
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: Well I’ve been put in charge of the school marching band, and it’s quite a responsibility.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: I’d like to talk it over with you.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: Go ahead.
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: You’d better start by giving me a bit of background.
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: Well the band has students in it from all years, so they’re aged 11 to 18, and there are about 50 of them altogether.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: It’s quite a popular activity within the school.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: I’ve never worked with a band of more than 20 before, and this is very different.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: I can imagine.
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: They aren’t really good enough to enter national band competitions, but they’re in a regional one later in the term.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: Even if they don’t win, and I don’t expect them to, hopefully it’ll be an incentive for them to try and improve.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: Yes, hopefully.
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: Well, now the town council’s organising a carnival in the summer, and the band has been asked to perform.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: If you ask me, they aren’t really up to it yet, and I need to get them functioning better as a band, and in a very short time.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: Have you been doing anything with them?
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: Apart from practising the music, I mean.
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: I played a recording I came across, of a drummer talking about how playing in a band had changed his life.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: I think it was an after-dinner speech.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: I thought it was pretty inspiring, because being in the band had stopped him from getting involved in crime.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: The students seemed to find it interesting, too.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: That’s good.
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: I’m planning to show them that old film from the 1940s ‘Strike Up the Band’, and talk about it with the students.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: What do you think?
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: Good idea.
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: As it’s about a school band, it might make the students realise how much they can achieve if they work together.
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: That’s what I’ve got in mind.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: I’m hoping I can take some of the band to a parade that’s going to take place next month.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: A couple of marching bands will be performing, and the atmosphere should be quite exciting.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: It depends on whether I can persuade the school to hire a coach or two to take us there.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: Mmm.
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: They sound like good ideas to me.
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: Thanks.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: Can I tell you about a few people in the band who I’m finding it quite difficult to cope with?
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: I’m sure you’ll have some ideas about what I can do.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: Go ahead.
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: There’s a flautist who says she loves playing in the band.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: We rehearse twice a week after school, but she’s hardly ever there.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: Then she looks for me the next day and gives me a very plausible reason – she says she had to help her mother, or she’s been ill, but to be honest, I don’t believe her.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: Oh dear!
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: Any more students with difficulties?
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: Plenty!
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: There’s a trumpeter who thinks she’s the best musician in the band, though she certainly isn’t.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: She’s always saying what she thinks other people should do, which makes my job pretty difficult.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: She sounds a bit of a nightmare!
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: You can say that again.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: One of the trombonists has got an impressive sense of rhythm, and could be an excellent musician – except that he has breathing difficulties, and he doesn’t really have enough breath for the trombone.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: He’d be much better off playing percussion, for instance, but he refuses to give up.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: So he ends up only playing half the notes.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: I suppose you have to admire his determination.
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: Maybe.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: One of the percussionists isn’t too bad, but he never seems to interact with other people, and he always rushes off as soon as the rehearsal ends.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: I don’t know if there are family reasons, or what.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: But it isn’t good in a band, where people really need to feel they’re part of a group.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: Hmm.
transcript.speaker: LIZZIE

transcript.text: There are others too, but at least that gives you an idea of what I’m up against.
transcript.speaker: JOE

transcript.text: Do you have any thoughts about what I can do, Lizzie?
transcript.speaker: JOE

groups.title: Concerts in university arts festival
groups.instruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

transcript.text: As you all know, the university is planning an arts festival for later this year, and here in the music department we’ve planned three concerts.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: These will be public performances, and the programme has just been finalised.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The theme of the festival is links between the UK and Australia, and this is reflected in the music: each concert will feature both British and Australian composers.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: I’ll tell you briefly about the Australian music, as you probably won’t be familiar with that.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The first concert will include music by Liza Lim, who was born in Perth, Western Australia, in 1966.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: As a child, Lim originally learned to play the piano – like so many children – and also the violin.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But when she was 11 her teachers encouraged her to start composing.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: She found this was her real strength, and she studied and later taught composition, both in Australia and in other countries.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: As a composer, she has received commissions from numerous orchestras, other performers and festivals in several countries.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Liza Lim’s compositions are vibrant and full of energy, and she often explores Asian and Australian Aboriginal cultural sources, including the native instrument, the didgeridoo: this is featured in a work called The Compass.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Her music is very expressive, so although it is complex, it has the power of connecting with audiences and performers alike.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In the festival we’re going to give a semi-staged performance of The Oresteia.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This is an opera in seven parts, based on the trilogy of ancient Greek tragedies by Aeschylus.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Lim composed this when she was in her mid-20s, and she also wrote the text, along with Barrie Kosky.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It’s performed by six singers, a dancer, and an orchestra that, as well as standard orchestral instruments, includes electric guitar, and a traditional Turkish stringed instrument.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Lim wrote that because the stories in the tragedies are not easy to tell, the sounds she creates are also disturbing, and they include breathing, sobbing, laughing and whistling.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The work lasts around 75 minutes, and the rest of the concert will consist of orchestral works by the British composers Ralph Vaughan Williams and Frederick Delius.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Moving on now to our second concert, this will begin with instrumental music by British composers – Benjamin Britten and Judith Weir.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: After the interval we’ll go to Australia for a piece by Ross Edwards: The Tower of Remoteness.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: According to Edwards, the inspiration for this piece came from nature, when he was sitting alone in the dry bed of a creek, overshadowed by the leaves of palm trees, listening to the birds and insects.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The Tower of Remoteness is scored for piano and clarinet.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Edwards says he realised years after writing the piece that he had subconsciously modelled its opening phrase on a bird call.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Ross Edwards was born in 1943 in Sydney, Australia, and studied at the Sydney Conservatorium of Music and the universities of Adelaide and Sydney.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: He’s well known in Australia, and in fact he’s one of the country’s most performed composers.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: He’s written a wide range of music, from symphonies and concertos to some composed specifically for children.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Edward’s music has been described as being ‘deeply connected to Australia’, and it can be regarded as a celebration of the diversity of cultures that Australia can be proud of.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The last of the three Australian composers to be represented in our festival is Carl Vine.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Born in 1954, Vine, like Liza Lim, comes from Perth, Western Australia.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: He took up the cornet at the age of five, switching to the piano five years later.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, he went to university to study physics, before changing to composition.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: After graduating he moved to Sydney and worked as a freelance pianist and composer.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Before long he had become prominent in Australia as a composer for dance, and in fact has written 25 scores of that type.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In our third concert, Vine will be represented by his music for the flag hand-over ceremony of the Olympics held in 1996.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This seven-minute orchestral piece was of course heard by millions of people worldwide, and we’ll hear it alongside works written by British composers Edward Elgar and, more recently, Thomas Adès.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
